The learning rate is the size of every step
gradients are unreliable; late in training they are close, and big steps would only shake them out again. A schedule changes the learning rate as training goes.

of the peak over the first

text.tspan: , a point walks along the half circle from the right end to the left, at a constant speed. The schedule multiplier
) is simply how far right its

shadow falls on the diameter. Near both ends the point moves almost vertically, so its shadow — the learning rate — barely changes; in the middle it moves almost horizontally, so the learning rate falls
fastest. That is the whole character of cosine decay: it stays near the peak for a while, drops through the middle of training, and eases gently into the end.

svg.text: the fall in learning rate from one step to the next (× 10⁻⁴)
both go from the peak to 0 over the same 190 steps (before the floor)
cosine: how much the rate falls each step
linear decay: the same fall every step

text.tspan: decay removes the same amount every step. Cosine removes almost nothing just after the peak, about
more than linear at the half-way point (π/
as fast), and almost nothing again at the end. So the model spends longer at a high rate, where it makes the most progress, and then settles slowly instead of being cut

E · Why warm up at all
’s first steps are as big as the learning rate — whatever the gradient says

divides each gradient by a running estimate of its size. On the very first step that estimate is the gradient itself, so the update of every single weight is exactly ± the learning rate — the full step, based on one noisy batch.
measured it: every output bias moved by exactly
. Over the first few steps the running
estimates are still built from very few batches and are unreliable.
Small steps while the estimates are still noisy
) — on the evidence of a single batch. Warmup lets the
’s running averages fill in before the steps become large. It matters most for
-type optimizers and for large models, and it costs almost nothing:
F · Why decay helps — an experiment
gradient descent with noisy gradients, under four schedules
A one-number "model" w must find the minimum of (w −
. Each step sees the true gradient plus random noise, as a real training batch does, and moves w by learning rate × gradient, with a peak rate of
with different noise; the chart is the average distance from the minimum at

svg.text: 300 runs per schedule, same noise seeds for every schedule · zoomed to 0–3: the first steps, when w is still far away, run off the top

text.tspan: All four schedules get close to the minimum quickly — early on they all take big steps. Then the difference appears: at a constant rate the noise keeps kicking w around the minimum by about
on average, forever. Every schedule that shrinks its steps settles closer, and the cosine ends closest (
), because it keeps the rate high

while w is far away and makes it small by the time only the noise is left to fight. This is a hand-set toy, not the Transformer — but the mechanism is the same one: late in training, a smaller step averages out the noise of each batch.
